title: The date is hard to read
script: Hi, I've looked at the poster on my phone. The book club title is clear, but I can barely read the meeting date. Could you make that easier to see? I'd like to keep the warm colors and the gold line. Thanks. Send me a quick preview before you share the final version.

gist.question: What is the organiser mainly asking for?

details.question: Where did the organiser view the poster?
What should remain?
choices: The warm colors and gold line.

phrases: I can read it only with difficulty.
The organiser wants a preview before the final post.
response: Respond to the readability problem, preserve what the organiser likes, and confirm the proof.
model: I’ll make the meeting date easier to read while keeping the warm palette and gold line. I’ll send a phone-size preview before sharing the final version.
speaker: Friend or organiser

context.why: Help a book club share a readable invitation.

A2.model: I’ll make the meeting date easier to read.

B1.model: I’ll make the meeting date clearer and keep the warm colors.

B2.model: I’ll make the meeting date easier to read while keeping the warm palette and gold line. I’ll send a phone-size preview before sharing the final version.

new_brief: A sports-club invitation has a clear title, but the meeting place is tiny. Suggest a readable change and ask what should stay.
independent_model: I’ll make the meeting date clearer and keep the warm colors. I would check the details with the intended audience before sharing.

title: “Make it pop” with a clue
script: Thanks for sending the draft. It feels close to our style, so I don't want to start again. Could you make the registration deadline pop a little more? The last day to sign up is the reason we're posting this. Please keep the logo where it is, and show me two options for the deadline rather than changing the whole design.

gist.question: What does “make it pop” mean here?

details.question: What must stay in its position?
How many deadline options does the organiser want?

phrases: Begin the design from the beginning.
Choose one action instead of another.
response: Clarify or confirm the requested emphasis and propose the two options.
model: I’ll keep the logo and overall style, then show two ways to emphasise the registration deadline. Would you prefer a size change in one version and a stronger color contrast in the other?
speaker: Friend or organiser

context.why: Clarify vague feedback on a club notice.

A2.model: I’ll make the registration deadline stand out.

B1.model: I’ll keep the style and show two ways to emphasise the deadline.

B2.model: I’ll keep the logo and overall style, then show two ways to emphasise the registration deadline. Would you prefer a size change in one version and a stronger color contrast in the other?

new_brief: A class notice says “make the room number pop”. Confirm what should change and propose two options.
independent_model: I’ll keep the style and show two ways to emphasise the deadline. I would check the details with the intended audience before sharing.

model: I’ll use the exact Arabic wording and keep the flower symbol. I’ll check the extra time needed before confirming when it will be ready, then send a preview for your cousin to review.

Please tell me what is ready, what you still need from us, and when you'll send the preview. We're working in different time zones, so please include the time zone in your message.

phrases: A draft good enough for a team conversation.
response: Give an honest progress update. If you do not know the meeting time, ask rather than invent a deadline.

script: I've compared the two mood boards. The bright version is fun, but our daytime visitors mostly come to read and have quiet conversations. I prefer the softer version for this poster. We can use a more energetic style for evening events later. For now, keep the invitation calm and make the practical details easy to find.

choices: A style chosen without considering the audience.

details.question: Who is this version for?
choices: Daytime visitors who read and talk quietly.

details.question: When might an energetic version be useful?

phrases: This is the current decision, not a permanent rule.
The information viewers need to act.
response: Recommend the current mood and distinguish it from the later campaign.
model: I’ll use the softer version for the daytime invitation and keep the practical details clear. We can develop an energetic version for evening events later. Could you confirm the opening time and location?
speaker: Friend or organiser

context.why: Choose a suitable tone for a library event.

title: Nike: simplicity and interpretation
script: Look at the Nike mark without the word. It is one curved shape, with a broader section at one end and a narrower tip at the other. The mark has very little internal detail, so we can still see its outline when it becomes small. To me, the curve suggests movement. That is an interpretation, rather than a fact the shape proves. In an analysis, describe the visible shape first, then explain what it may suggest and how it works at a smaller size.

gist.question: What does this analysis connect?
choices: A simple shape, small-size use, and a possible reading.
A comparison of two typefaces in the wordmark.
A recommendation to add more internal detail.

details.question: Which observation is visible?
choices: The outline has very little internal detail.
The outline contains several separate small shapes.
The main feature is a textured surface.

details.question: How is “movement” presented?
choices: As the documented intention of the original designer.
As the only reading the audience can have.

phrases: The speaker qualifies a personal interpretation.
response: Analyse the mark in three sentences: visible fact, possible reading, practical test.
model: I notice a single curved shape with little internal detail. To me, it suggests movement. I would test its outline at a small size before making a similar design choice for a new client.

context.why: Describe a familiar logo and qualify what it may suggest.

A2.model: The mark is one curved shape.

B1.model: The simple curve may suggest movement, but that is an interpretation.

B2.model: I notice a single curved shape with little internal detail. To me, it suggests movement. I would test its outline at a small size before making a similar design choice for a new client.

new_brief: A new club symbol uses a simple curved line. Describe one visible feature, qualify a possible meaning, and suggest a small-size check.
independent_model: The simple curve may suggest movement, but that is an interpretation. I would check the details with the intended audience before sharing.

title: Microsoft: shape, space, and repetition
script: The Microsoft symbol uses four colored squares. They sit in a two-by-two arrangement, with clear gaps between them. The repeated square shape and the regular spacing make the group feel organised to me. Notice that repetition does not require one color: the shape repeats while the colors differ. We can describe those choices without claiming that each color has one universal meaning. When analysing a new mark, ask which features repeat, which features change, and what remains recognisable when the mark is small.

gist.question: What repeats in this symbol?
choices: The square shape and regular arrangement.
A single color across every part.
A shading effect that makes the squares look three-dimensional.

details.question: How many squares are there?
What differs between the squares?
choices: The colors differ while the square shape repeats.
The shapes differ while every color stays the same.
The gaps disappear as the colors change.

phrases: One feature changes while another stays consistent.
response: Describe two elements and one principle, then give a small-size test.
model: The symbol uses four square shapes with different colors. Repetition and regular spacing connect them as a group. I would test whether the gaps remain clear at a small size.

context.why: Describe a familiar logo and qualify what it may suggest.

A2.model: Four squares repeat in a regular arrangement.

B1.model: The repeated squares and regular gaps make an organised group.

B2.model: The symbol uses four square shapes with different colors. Repetition and regular spacing connect them as a group. I would test whether the gaps remain clear at a small size.

new_brief: A student group symbol uses three repeated circles in different colors. Explain what repeats and what changes without assigning a universal meaning to each color.
independent_model: The repeated squares and regular gaps make an organised group. I would check the details with the intended audience before sharing.

title: Amazon: the arrow as a visual clue
script: Look beneath the Amazon wordmark. The orange curved arrow starts under the letter A and points toward the letter Z. Those are visible details we can point to. Its curved shape may also look like a smile to a viewer. That is a reading of the shape, not proof of how everyone will respond. In an organiser explanation, separate what you can see from the meaning you suggest. Then ask whether the detail still reads clearly when the wordmark is small or shown in one color.

gist.question: What distinction does the speaker make?
choices: A fixed meaning for every orange shape.
A recommendation to replace the arrow with a straight line.

details.question: Which letters does the speaker identify?
Which description is an interpretation?
choices: The arrow may resemble a smile.
The arrow is beneath the wordmark.
The arrow has an orange color.

phrases: Qualifies a resemblance rather than guaranteeing it.
response: Point to the arrow, describe its direction, and qualify one possible reading.
model: I can see an orange curved arrow beneath the wordmark, pointing from A toward Z. It may resemble a smile. I would check whether that detail remains clear at a small size and in one color.

context.why: Describe a familiar logo and qualify what it may suggest.

A2.model: The curved arrow may look like a smile.

B1.model: The arrow goes from A toward Z and may also look like a smile.

B2.model: I can see an orange curved arrow beneath the wordmark, pointing from A toward Z. It may resemble a smile. I would check whether that detail remains clear at a small size and in one color.

new_brief: A library symbol has a curved arrow beneath its name. Separate an observation from an interpretation, then say what you would check at a small size.
independent_model: The arrow goes from A toward Z and may also look like a smile. I would check the details with the intended audience before sharing.

title: McDonald’s: recognisable form with few details
script: The supplied McDonald's mark uses two joined arches that make an M-like shape. The color is yellow, and there is very little extra detail inside the mark. We can discuss shape and color as elements, and simplicity as a principle. Familiarity may help us recognise this particular mark, so recognition alone does not prove that any similar yellow shape would work for a new business. A designer still needs to check distinctiveness, clarity, and whether the mark fits the organiser's actual audience.

details.question: What basic shape does the speaker describe?
choices: Two joined arches forming an M-like mark.
Two separate circles forming a wordmark.
Four colored squares forming a grid.

details.question: Why is familiarity mentioned?
choices: Knowing the brand already can help recognition.
Familiarity proves the mark works for every new audience.
Familiarity removes the need for small-size testing.

phrases: Few internal features to distract from the main shape.
response: Describe the mark and explain why a new organiser’s logo needs its own audience test.
model: I notice two joined arches and a yellow color. The simple shape has few internal details, but familiarity also helps me recognise it. A new mark still needs its own clarity and audience test.

context.why: Describe a familiar logo and qualify what it may suggest.

A2.model: The mark has two yellow arches.

B1.model: The simple yellow arches are recognisable, partly through familiarity.

B2.model: I notice two joined arches and a yellow color. The simple shape has few internal details, but familiarity also helps me recognise it. A new mark still needs its own clarity and audience test.

new_brief: A new café proposes two yellow arches for its symbol. Explain why familiarity alone does not show that the new symbol is distinctive or suitable.
independent_model: The simple yellow arches are recognisable, partly through familiarity. I would check the details with the intended audience before sharing.
